So not paying the new rent can weaken it; say so.

What the tenant can do about an increase alone, before any case: not settled. One: 83.64(2) makes it only a defense, so there is nothing to raise until a case. The other: 83.64(1) makes the increase unlawful, "Any right or duty declared in this part is enforceable by civil action." (83.54), and a party may recover damages for a failure to comply with "this part" (83.55).

## If the tenant already paid it

"if the tenant pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord" (83.56(5)(a)), the tenant "waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." (83.56(5)(a)).

Ask what they knew when they paid, and set it beside "actual knowledge" (83.56(5)(a)). Whether paying a raised rent gives up the extra, or changes the rent from then on, is not settled, so going back to the lease's rent and getting the extra back are not settled either. Start the answer there. One: paying with knowledge gives up a suit over those months and may show the tenant agreed. The other: an increase the lease never allowed is not rent "due" (83.43(12)), a clause requiring a signed change still stands, and the extra can be claimed under 83.55, with each later month a "subsequent or continuing noncompliance" (83.56(5)(a)). Amounts and court steps are outside this tool; do not total them.

## If the landlord treats it as unpaid rent

- **A written demand.** "If the tenant fails to pay rent when due and the default continues for 3 days, excluding Saturday, Sunday, and legal holidays, after delivery of written demand by the landlord for payment of the rent or possession of the premises, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement." (83.56(3)). This tool does not count those days; the demand states them. Say not to ignore it.
- **Taking the old rent.** A landlord "does not waive the right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance by accepting partial rent for the period." (83.56(5)(a)). So taking it does not mean the landlord gave in. "If partial rent is accepted after posting the notice for nonpayment, the landlord must:" (83.56(5)(a)) give a receipt with the date, the amount, and the balance before filing; or put the amount in the court's registry on filing; or post a new 3-day notice (83.56(5)(a)). Whether the lease's rent is "partial" at all is the dispute.
- **No court case, no removal.** "The landlord shall not recover possession of a dwelling unit except:" (83.59(3)) through a court case, or when the tenant gave up or abandoned the home (83.59(3)). The landlord "shall not prevent the tenant from gaining reasonable access to the dwelling unit by any means" (83.67(2)).
- **A case filed.** Say this first. The tenant must pay into the registry "the accrued rent as alleged in the complaint or as determined by the court and the rent that accrues during the pendency of the proceeding, when due." (83.60(2)). "Failure of the tenant to pay the rent into the registry of the court or to file a motion to determine the amount of rent to be paid into the registry within 5 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays, after the date of service of process constitutes an absolute waiver of the tenant’s defenses other than payment, and the landlord is entitled to an immediate default judgment for removal of the tenant with a writ of possession to issue without further notice or hearing thereon." (83.60(2)). When the amount is what they dispute, the motion is the way to say so: "If a motion to determine rent is filed, documentation in support of the allegation that the rent as alleged in the complaint is in error is required." (83.60(2)). A tenant with subsidized rent deposits "only that portion of the full rent for which they are responsible" (83.60(2)). Give the 5 days and what they leave out, but never a calendar date for them; "The clerk shall notify the tenant of such requirement in the summons." (83.60(2)).
- **Defenses.** The tenant "may raise any other defense, whether legal or equitable, that he or she may have, including the defense of retaliatory conduct in accordance with s. 83.64" (83.60(1)(a)). The winner may recover attorney fees and court costs (83.48). Other court steps are outside this tool.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Stating a notice period or a cap for rent increases as the law.
- Saying a landlord may raise the rent during a set term with no clause and no agreement, or calling the lease's own rent steps an increase.
- Treating 83.57's 30 days as settled for an increase, saying flatly that no notice is needed, or saying flatly that a letter alone changes the rent with no set end date.
- Saying an increase is retaliation because it followed a complaint, or leaving out good faith or being treated differently.
- Telling a tenant they can stop paying rent altogether, explaining a case without 83.60(2), or giving a calendar date for its 5 days.
- Applying a local rent rule from memory.
- Writing any date count_days did not give you, or counting how long something has lasted or how long until a date. Setting a date from the facts beside a date count_days gave is not counting.

tool_calls.result:
Loaded lease_ending. Its instructions:

# Lease ending

Rests on 83.575 (a set end date), 83.57 and 83.46 (no set end date), 83.58, 83.59, and 83.67 (staying on, no lockout), 83.56 and 83.505 (delivering notices), 83.49 (the 7 days' notice, the deposit), 83.595 and 83.45 (limits on charges), 83.43 and 83.64 (good faith, retaliation), 83.60 (if sued), 83.47, 83.55, and 83.48 (void clauses, damages, attorney fees), and 83.5615 (foreclosure). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

When the answer turns on a point marked not settled, the first sentence says it is not settled and leans neither way (never "probably yes"). Every point marked not settled gets both readings, and you choose neither.

## First, whether this applies

- Load who_the_law_covers, unless the facts already hold school_housing.
- The tenant wants to move out well before the end date: load wants_to_leave_early.
- The landlord's notice names something the tenant did: load notice_received_violation.
- A higher rent comes with the renewal: load rent_increased too.
- After the move, the deposit: load deposit_not_returned.
- A new owner after a foreclosure says to leave: 83.5615 calls for a notice "at least 90 days before the effective date of the notice" (83.5615(2)(a)) and protects a bona fide lease's remaining term, with limits (83.5615(2)(b)). Its note says it takes effect upon the repeal of a federal act, and the stored text does not say whether that has happened; say this needs checking.

## What the lease adds

Read the whole lease, addenda included, for: the end date; any notice before leaving at the end; any notice from the landlord; any charge for missing a notice; renewal; staying after the end; how notices go; and what move-out requires. Quote each clause and cite it.

A clause that renews the lease if no notice is given: say what it says. Whether option 1's conditions for a charge reach it is not settled. One: it is a way of charging for a missed notice, so the landlord's own notice is needed first. The other: a renewal is not a charge, and 83.575(2) speaks only of liquidated damages, so the clause stands.

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- lease_end_date: the date a set term ends. period_end: with no set end date, the last day of the rent period they ask about. next_period_end: the last day of the rent period after that.
- planned_move_out: the date they plan to leave.
- tenant_notice_delivered: the date their notice reached the landlord, and how it went.
- landlord_notice_delivered: the date a paper from the landlord about the end reached them, how it came, and what it lists. If mailed or left at the door, landlord_notice_sent: the date it was mailed or left.
- permission: what the landlord has said or done about their staying, and whether it is in writing. rent_after_end: any rent paid or taken for a time after the end.
- eviction_filed: whether a case has been filed, and whether they were served. complaint_date: the date of any complaint before the landlord acted, and what it was.

## Which kind of tenancy

- **A set end date:** 83.575. Options 1 to 3, and "When the landlord will not renew".
- **No set end date:** 83.57. "If the rental agreement contains no provision as to duration of the tenancy, the duration is determined by the periods for which the rent is payable." (83.46(2)). A home that comes with a job goes by the pay periods (83.46(3)). Option 4, and "When the landlord ends a tenancy with no set end date".
- **Stayed on with permission after a set term:** read the lease's clause on staying. With none, 83.575(3) points to the 83.57(3) notice; see option 2.

Part II names no right to renew.

## How a notice is delivered

This covers a landlord's notice under 83.575, and either side's notice under 83.57. A tenant's own notice before leaving at the end of a set term goes as the lease says; 83.575(1) names no way for it. The ways: "The delivery of the written notices required by subsections (1)-(3) shall be by mailing, delivering a true copy thereof, e-mailing in accordance with s. 83.505 , or, if the tenant is absent from the premises, by leaving a copy thereof at the residence." (83.56(4)).

- **Handed over:** delivered that day.
- **Mailed, or left at the door while the tenant was away:** a way the statute names, but not settled which day counts. One: the mailing or the leaving is the delivery. The other: a paper is delivered when it reaches the person. For a landlord's notice, set both landlord_notice_sent and landlord_notice_delivered beside the date. For the tenant's own notice, handing it over or mailing it early meets both.
- **E-mail under the signed addendum:** only with every condition of 83.505(1); then it is "deemed delivered at the time it is sent, unless the e-mail is returned to the sender as undeliverable." (83.505(4)).
- **A text, a portal message, an e-mail with no addendum, or a copy left at the door while the tenant was home:** not a way 83.56(4) names. Not settled whether it still counts because it reached the person. One: delivery "shall be by" (83.56(4)) the ways named, so it is not the required notice. The other: "This section does not preclude service of notices by any other means permitted by law." (83.505(6)). If there is still time, sending it again by hand or by mail meets both.
- **Spoken:** the statute asks for a written notice in these cases. No notice has been given.

A lease clause on notices adds to this: a way that meets both the clause and the statute is safest. Say what the clause says.

## Option 1: leave at the end of a set term

1. **Does the lease ask for notice?** The lease "may contain a provision requiring the tenant to notify the landlord within a specified period before vacating the premises at the end of the rental agreement" (83.575(1)). No such clause: the stored text asks for no notice before leaving on the end date. Say so plainly.
2. **Is the clause one the statute allows?** Two limits, each with its own question. Say what is not settled, and that notice by the date given meets both readings.
   - The length: "A rental agreement may not require less than 30 days’ notice or more than 60 days’ notice from either the tenant or the landlord." (83.575(1)). A clause outside it: not settled what follows. One: the statute does not rewrite such a clause, so no notice is owed under it. The other: a clause is void only "to the extent that it" (83.47(1)) takes away what part II gives, so it stands at the limit. Over 60 days: the date is count_days(lease_end_date, -60). Under 30 days: count_days(lease_end_date, -30).
   - The landlord's half: the clause must also require "the landlord to notify the tenant in a manner prescribed by s. 83.56 (4) within such notice period if the rental agreement will not be renewed." (83.575(1)). A clause without it: not settled what follows. One: the statute allows the clause only "if such provision also requires" (83.575(1)) that, so no notice is owed under it. The other: the statute does not say the tenant's promise falls away, so it still binds. The date is the lease's own.
3. **The last day.** If the clause gives a number of days N: count_days(lease_end_date, -N). If it is in months, give the lease's words; the tool counts days only.

Leaving before the last day of the term: "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement" (83.49(5)), a tenant leaving "before the expiration of the term specified in the rental agreement" (83.49(5)) gives the 7 days' notice: count_days(planned_move_out, -7), with planned_move_out the day they will actually leave (if they name no earlier day, give no date), in writing, by certified mail or personal delivery, with an address where the tenant can be reached (83.49(5)). Read the lease for a clause on notice before leaving. Rent through the end date is still owed under the lease.

**What missing the notice costs.** A lease "may provide that if a tenant fails to give the required notice before vacating the premises at the end of the rental agreement, the tenant may be liable for liquidated damages as specified in the rental agreement" (83.575(2)). All of these must be met for that charge:

1. **The tenant missed a required notice.** They gave it in time, or the clause falls under step 2's limits: say so, with step 2's readings.
2. **The lease sets the charge.** No charge in the lease: this part does not apply.
3. **The landlord sent its own written notice first,** "specifying the tenant’s obligations under the notification provision contained in the rental agreement and the date the rental agreement is terminated." (83.575(2)), and it "must list all fees, penalties, and other charges applicable to the tenant under this subsection." (83.575(2)). No such notice, or one that leaves any of these out: not met, and the charge is not owed. Say so plainly.
4. **Delivered a way the statute names** (see "How a notice is delivered").
5. **In time.** "within 15 days before the start of the notification period contained in the rental agreement." (83.575(2)). The start: count_days(lease_end_date, -N). Fifteen days before it: count_days(lease_end_date, -(N+15)); pass the sum as one number. What the words ask is not settled. One: the notice must come during the 15 days that end when the period starts, not earlier. The other: it must come no later than 15 days before the period starts, and earlier is also in time. Set the date it came beside both dates:
   - Exactly on the earlier date: in time under both. Say so plainly.
   - Between the two dates: in time under the first reading, too late under the second.
   - Before the earlier date: too early under the first reading, in time under the second.
   - After the start: too late under both, and the charge is not owed. Say so plainly.

The limit on fees for leaving early does not apply here: 83.595(4) "does not apply if the breach is failure to give notice as provided in s. 83.575 ." (83.595(4)(b)). Do not apply its two months' rent limit or its separate addendum to this charge. Part II sets no number for this charge; a court may refuse or limit an "unconscionable" (83.45(1)) clause, and that is for a court. Apart from this charge, a landlord may claim damages for a failure to follow the lease (83.55); amounts are outside this tool.

Moving out: read what the lease requires. Any claim on the deposit goes through the deposit steps; load deposit_not_returned after the move.

## Option 2: stay on with the landlord's agreement

A new lease or a written agreement says what the rent and the term are. Read the lease's clause on staying and what it requires. "If the tenant remains on the premises with the permission of the landlord after the rental agreement has terminated and fails to give notice required under s. 83.57 (3), the tenant is liable to the landlord for an additional 1 month’s rent." (83.575(3)). So a tenant who stays with permission gives option 4's notice when they leave. Say so. Asking the landlord for its answer in writing settles what permission there is.

## Option 3: stay without permission

Say the risk plainly. A tenant who "holds over and continues in possession of the dwelling unit or any part thereof after the expiration of the rental agreement without the permission of the landlord" (83.58) can be sued for possession (83.58), and "The landlord may also recover double the amount of rent due on the dwelling unit, or any part thereof, for the period during which the tenant refuses to surrender possession." (83.58). Do not total it. For a tenancy ended by a notice under 83.57, whether it has reached its "expiration" (83.58) is not settled. One: a tenancy ended by proper notice has expired, so double rent can apply. The other: expiration means the end of a term, and 83.57 speaks of a tenancy "terminated" (83.57).

But the end date does not put them out by itself: "The landlord shall not recover possession of a dwelling unit except:" (83.59(3)) through a court case, or when the tenant gave up or abandoned the home (83.59(3)). The landlord "shall not prevent the tenant from gaining reasonable access to the dwelling unit by any means" (83.67(2)), changing the locks included, and if it does or cuts a utility it is liable for "actual and consequential damages or 3 months’ rent, whichever is greater, and costs, including attorney’s fees." (83.67(6)).

What counts as permission, when the landlord said nothing or took rent for a time after the end, is not settled. One: taking rent for that time is permission, since a landlord that "accepts rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the tenant" (83.56(5)(a)) gives up acting on it. Then 83.58 does not apply, and 83.575(3) and option 4's notice do. The other: permission must be given, and taking rent alone does not change a tenant who holds over, since the same sentence leaves open "any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." (83.56(5)(a)). Set what the landlord did and any lease clause on consent beside both. Getting the landlord's answer in writing settles it either way.

## Option 4: end a tenancy with no set end date

"A tenancy without a specific duration, as defined in s. 83.46 (2) or (3), may be terminated by either party giving written notice in the manner provided in s. 83.56 (4)" (83.57). No reason is named. The notice, by rent period: year to year, 60 days before the end of the year's period (83.57(1)); quarter to quarter, 30 days (83.57(2)); month to month, "not less than 30 days’ notice prior to the end of any monthly period" (83.57(3)); week to week, 7 days (83.57(4)).

1. **The last day.** Month to month: count_days(period_end, -30). If that has passed, the tenant can give notice for the next period instead: count_days(next_period_end, -30). Whether a notice that came too late for the end it names still works for a later period is not settled; give the two readings under "When the landlord ends a tenancy with no set end date". For another rent period, use its number of days.
2. **Written, and delivered a way the statute names** (see "How a notice is delivered").
3. **The 7 days' notice too.** "Except when otherwise provided by the terms of a written rental agreement" (83.49(5)), it also applies to "any tenant who vacates or abandons premises which are the subject of a tenancy from week to week, month to month, quarter to quarter, or year to year" (83.49(5)). It must be written, by certified mail or personal delivery, with an address, at least 7 days before leaving: count_days(planned_move_out, -7). Read the lease for a clause on notice before leaving. One notice by hand or certified mail, with the address, in time for both, meets both. Missing it "relieves the landlord of the notice requirement of paragraph (3)(a) but does not waive any right the tenant may have to the security deposit or any part of it." (83.49(5)).

A tenant who stayed on with permission after a set term and misses the 83.57(3) notice owes the extra month's rent (83.575(3)). For a tenancy that was month to month from the start, that is not settled. One: (3) names the month-to-month notice, so it applies. The other: the section is about a tenancy "with specific duration" (83.575), so it does not.

## When the landlord will not renew

The tenant has a set end date and the landlord says it will not renew. Part II names no reason it must give.

- **The lease has a notice clause with the landlord's half.** The last day for the landlord: count_days(lease_end_date, -N). If the clause is outside the limit, set the notice beside the lease's date and the limit's, as in option 1. If it is in months, give the lease's words. In a named way, on or before the last day: met, and the lease ends on its date. Say so plainly. Late, or not in a named way: what follows is not settled. One: the lease still ends on its date by its own words, and the landlord's miss is a failure of the lease, for damages at most (83.55). The other: the clause makes the landlord's notice the way a lease is not renewed, so without it the landlord cannot hold the tenant to the end date. Say what the lease says about renewal.
- **The lease has no such clause.** The stored text asks for no notice from the landlord before a set term ends. Say so plainly.
- Either way, see option 3 for staying, and "After a complaint" below.

## When the landlord ends a tenancy with no set end date

Set the landlord's notice beside option 4's rule. Month to month: count_days(period_end, -30), with period_end the last day of the rent period holding the date the notice names. If it was mailed or left at the door, use both dates, as "How a notice is delivered" says.

- **Written, in a named way, on or before that date:** met, and the tenancy ends at period_end. Say so plainly, and go to option 3 for staying.
- **Too late for that period, or naming a date that is not the end of a rent period:** it does not meet the rule for that date. Say so plainly. Whether it works for a later period is not settled. One: it is still written notice, so if it came by count_days(next_period_end, -30) the tenancy can end at next_period_end. The other: it names an end the statute does not allow, so it is not the required notice, and the landlord must give a new one.
- **By text, by portal, or spoken:** see "How a notice is delivered".

Whichever it is, say not to ignore it, and that the landlord still needs a court case (option 3).

## After a complaint

"It is unlawful for a landlord to discriminatorily increase a tenant’s rent or decrease services to a tenant, or to bring or threaten to bring an action for possession or other civil action, primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant." (83.64(1)). Not renewing, or giving 83.57's notice, is not named there. Whether either is covered by itself is not settled. One: it is a step toward the action the rule names, so it is covered. The other: the rule lists the landlord's acts, and this is not one.

A tenant sued for possession can raise it as a defense (83.64(2)). The examples of what is protected include a complaint to a code agency (83.64(1)(a)), a tenant organization (83.64(1)(b)), and a complaint under 83.56(1) (83.64(1)(c)), and they are only examples (83.64(1)). The tenant must have acted in good faith (83.64(1)), and "“Good faith” means honesty in fact in the conduct or transaction concerned." (83.43(8)). They must be treated differently (83.64(4)), and the landlord must have acted primarily to retaliate, which is for a court.

It falls away "if the landlord proves that the eviction is for good cause." (83.64(3)), whose examples include "violation of the terms of this chapter." (83.64(3)). Whether staying after the end is that kind of violation is not settled. One: holding over without permission is what 83.58 addresses, so it is good cause. The other: that would leave the defense nothing to do whenever a lease has ended. Give the dates as the tenant gave them; never count the days between them.

## If the landlord sues

Say this first when a case has been filed. "In an action by the landlord for possession of a dwelling unit, if the tenant interposes any defense other than payment, including, but not limited to, the defense of a defective 3-day notice, the tenant shall pay into the registry of the court the accrued rent as alleged in the complaint or as determined by the court and the rent that accrues during the pendency of the proceeding, when due." (83.60(2)). "Failure of the tenant to pay the rent into the registry of the court or to file a motion to determine the amount of rent to be paid into the registry within 5 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays, after the date of service of process constitutes an absolute waiver of the tenant’s defenses other than payment, and the landlord is entitled to an immediate default judgment for removal of the tenant with a writ of possession to issue without further notice or hearing thereon." (83.60(2)). A motion needs papers showing why the amount is wrong (83.60(2)). A tenant with subsidized rent deposits only their own share (83.60(2)). Give the 5 days and what they leave out, but never a calendar date for them; "The clerk shall notify the tenant of such requirement in the summons." (83.60(2)). The winner may recover attorney fees and court costs (83.48). Other court steps are outside this tool.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Saying a lease's notice clause binds the tenant without checking the landlord's half and the 30 to 60 days.
- Saying a tenant owes the charge for missing a notice without every condition of 83.575(2), or applying 83.595(4)'s limits to it.
- Saying the tenant must be out on the end date, or that the landlord may then remove them without a court case.
- Stating double rent as owed while what the landlord said or did leaves permission in doubt, or applying 83.575(3) with no permission.
- Applying 83.57's 30 days to a set term still running, or treating a late notice as good for the date it names.
- Saying part II gives a right to renew, or requires a reason for not renewing.
- Giving a calendar date for the 5 days in 83.60(2).
- Writing any date count_days did not give you, or counting how long something has lasted or how long until a date. Setting a date from the facts beside a date count_days gave is not counting.

cited.words: 83.425 Preemption. — The regulation of residential tenancies, the landlord-tenant relationship, and all other matters covered under this part are preempted to the state. This section supersedes any local government regulations on matters covered under this part, including, but not limited to, the screening process used by a landlord in approving tenancies; security deposits; rental agreement applications and fees associated with such applications; terms and conditions of rental agreements; the rights and responsibilities of the landlord and tenant; disclosures concerning the premises, the dwelling unit, the rental agreement, or the rights and responsibilities of the landlord and tenant; fees charged by the landlord; or notice requirements.

(1) A rental agreement with a specific duration may contain a provision requiring the tenant to notify the landlord within a specified period before vacating the premises at the end of the rental agreement, if such provision also requires the landlord to notify the tenant in a manner prescribed by s. 83.56 (4) within such notice period if the rental agreement will not be renewed. A rental agreement may not require less than 30 days’ notice or more than 60 days’ notice from either the tenant or the landlord.

83.58 Remedies; tenant holding over. — If the tenant holds over and continues in possession of the dwelling unit or any part thereof after the expiration of the rental agreement without the permission of the landlord, the landlord may recover possession of the dwelling unit in the manner provided for in s. 83.59 . The landlord may also recover double the amount of rent due on the dwelling unit, or any part thereof, for the period during which the tenant refuses to surrender possession.

(3) The landlord shall not recover possession of a dwelling unit except: (a) In an action for possession under subsection (2) or other civil action in which the issue of right of possession is determined; (b) When the tenant has surrendered possession of the dwelling unit to the landlord; (c) When the tenant has abandoned the dwelling unit. In the absence of actual knowledge of abandonment, it shall be presumed that the tenant has abandoned the dwelling unit if he or she is absent from the premises for a period of time equal to one-half the time for periodic rental payments. However, this presumption does not apply if the rent is current or the tenant has notified the landlord, in writing, of an intended absence; or (d) When the last remaining tenant of a dwelling unit is deceased, personal property remains on the premises, rent is unpaid, at least 60 days have elapsed following the date of death, and the landlord has not been notified in writing of the existence of a probate estate or of the name and address of a personal representative. This paragraph does not apply to a dwelling unit used in connection with a federally administered or regulated housing program, including programs under s. 202, s. 221(d)(3) and (4), s. 236, or s. 8 of the National Housing Act, as amended.

(2) A landlord of any dwelling unit governed by this part shall not prevent the tenant from gaining reasonable access to the dwelling unit by any means, including, but not limited to, changing the locks or using any bootlock or similar device.

(1) It is unlawful for a landlord to discriminatorily increase a tenant’s rent or decrease services to a tenant, or to bring or threaten to bring an action for possession or other civil action, primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant. In order for the tenant to raise the defense of retaliatory conduct, the tenant must have acted in good faith. Not on these terms. Section 11 lets your landlord raise the rent during the lease, but only with at least 60 days' written notice. Your letter was handed to you on March 2 and set the new rent to start April 1. That is less than 60 days, so section 11 doesn't support an April 1 start. Your rent stays at $1,050 for now, and you should keep paying that amount in full and on time. Your landlord can still raise the rent later if it follows section 11.

Has your landlord raised your rent at any other time since your lease began on August 1, 2025?

DETAILS

### Does Florida law let a landlord raise rent during a lease?
- Florida's landlord-tenant law (Fla. Stat. ch. 83, part II) has no section that lets a landlord raise rent during a fixed lease term. It also has no section that sets a notice period for increases or caps how much rent can go up.
- So your lease controls. Your lease runs through July 31, 2026, and the new rent would start April 1, which is inside that term.
- Local rules can't change this. Section 83.425 says these matters are "preempted to the state." I have no local rent rule in this tool, and I haven't applied one.

### What does your lease allow?
- Section 4 sets your rent at "$1,050.00 per month."
- Section 11 says: "Landlord may raise the rent during the term, no more than once, by giving Tenant at least 60 days' written notice delivered to the apartment."
- Section 10 says the lease "may be changed only in writing signed by Landlord and Tenant." You told me you signed nothing.

### Did the letter meet section 11?
- **Written, delivered to the apartment:** You said the letter was handed to you at your apartment door. That appears to meet this part.
- **At least 60 days:** This part is not met. For an April 1 start, the last day to give notice was January 31, 2026. That date has passed.
- **No more than once:** I don't know yet. That is why I asked my question.
- **Earliest start:** Counting 60 days from the March 2 delivery, the earliest start is May 1, 2026. Your letter named April 1, not May 1. I can't tell you whether your landlord must send a new letter for a later start.

### What should you do now?
- Keep paying $1,050 by the due date. Keep the letter, your lease, and proof of each payment.
- You can tell your landlord in writing that you don't agree to the April 1 increase. Quote section 4 and the 60-day requirement in section 11. Under lease section 7, deliver it by hand to the office at 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A, or send it there by certified mail.
- There is a risk. Your landlord might treat $1,050 as short rent and send a written demand for the difference. Under section 83.56(3), if rent isn't paid and "the default continues for 3 days, excluding Saturday, Sunday, and legal holidays, after delivery of written demand," the landlord "may terminate the rental agreement." Don't ignore a demand like that.
- Your landlord can't remove you without a court case. See sections 83.59(3) and 83.67(2).
- If you pay the higher rent, you may give up the right to challenge it. Section 83.56(5)(a) says that paying rent "with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord" waives certain rights for that noncompliance. Whether that would apply here is not settled.

# Rent increased

Rests on 83.46 (rent, tenancies with no set term), 83.43 (what rent is, good faith), 83.57 (ending a tenancy with no set term), 83.64 (retaliation), 83.425 (local rules), 83.56 (unpaid rent, rent paid, notices), 83.60 (if sued), 83.55 and 83.54 (damages, suits), 83.44 and 83.45 (good faith, unfair clauses), 83.48 (attorney fees), 83.51 and 83.491 (trash, a fee in place of a deposit), 83.59 and 83.67 (no lockout), and 83.505 (e-mail notices). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

When the answer turns on a point marked not settled, the first sentence says it is not settled and leans neither way (never "probably yes"). Every point marked not settled gets all its readings, and you choose none.

## First, whether this applies

- Load who_the_law_covers, unless the facts already hold school_housing.
- Part II has no section that sets how much notice a rent increase needs, and none that limits how much rent may go up. Say so plainly when asked. Never state a notice period or a cap as the law.
- Local rules: "The regulation of residential tenancies, the landlord-tenant relationship, and all other matters covered under this part are preempted to the state." (83.425), and the section supersedes local rules on matters including "fees charged by the landlord; or notice requirements." (83.425). The stored text holds no local rent rule. Never apply one from memory.
- Rent paid through a program (a voucher, public housing): the program's own rules are not stored. Say they may limit this, and that they are outside this tool.
- The increase comes with an offer to renew, or the tenant would rather leave: load lease_ending too.

## What the lease adds

Read the whole lease, addenda included, for: the rent, the term, any clause on the rent changing, how the lease may be changed, any charges, staying after the end, and how notices go to the landlord. Quote each clause and cite it.

- **Rent steps set in the lease from the start** (so much until a date, then more): that is the lease's rent, not an increase. Say so.
- **A clause letting the landlord raise the rent during the term:** set the increase beside the clause's conditions (how much notice, how it is given, how much, how often). If it gives a number of days N: the last day to give notice for the start date named is count_days(new_rent_starts, -N), and the earliest start from the notice given is count_days(increase_delivered, N). All conditions met: the rent goes up as the lease says; say so plainly. Any not met: the clause does not support this increase on these terms; say so plainly. The rent stays where it is for now and the tenant keeps paying it, but the landlord can still raise it by meeting the clause, so say that too. Option 1's plain answer is for a lease with no such clause. A clause with no limit at all: say what it says, that it carries "an obligation of good faith in its performance or enforcement." (83.44), and that whether it is unfair enough to be "unconscionable" (83.45(1)) is for a court.
- **A new charge** (an amenity fee, a trash fee): the same questions as for rent. The lease provides it: owed as the lease says. It does not: during a set term the landlord cannot add it alone, any more than it can raise the rent. A fee counts as rent only if it is "designated as rent in a written rental agreement." (83.43(12)). That matters because a demand under 83.56(3) and the registry under 83.60(2) speak of rent.
  - Trash: in a unit other than a single-family home or duplex, "Garbage removal and outside receptacles therefor." (83.51(2)(a)) falls to the landlord "Unless otherwise agreed in writing" (83.51(2)(a)), though the rental agreement may put the charges on the tenant (83.51(2)(e)).
  - A fee in place of a security deposit: "The amount of the fee, which may not be increased during the term of the rental agreement." (83.491(4)(a)).

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- new_rent: the new amount. increase_delivered: the date word of it reached them, and how it came (handed over, mail, portal, text, spoken). new_rent_starts: the date it is said to start.
- lease_end_date: the date the lease ends, if it has one. period_end: the last day of the rent period before the new rent starts. next_period_end: the last day of the rent period after that.
- agreed: whether they signed anything or said yes. paid_new_rent: whether they have paid the new amount, for which months, and what they knew about the lease when they paid.
- complaint_date: the date of any complaint or similar step before the increase, and what it was. others_rent: what they know about other tenants' rent.
- rent_demand: any written demand for rent, and its date. eviction_filed: whether a case has been filed, and whether they were served.

## Which kind of increase

Settle this first. With a set end date, call count_days(lease_end_date, 0) and set new_rent_starts beside the date it gives.

- A set end date, and the new rent starts on or before it: option 1.
- A set end date, and the new rent starts after it: option 2.
- No set end date, or the tenant stayed on after a set term with the landlord's permission: option 3. With no term stated, "the duration is determined by the periods for which the rent is payable." (83.46(2)). Stayed on without permission, or in doubt: load lease_ending too.

Any kind: option 4 if the tenant did something first that the landlord may be answering, such as a complaint or joining a tenant group, and the two parts after it if they fit.

## Option 1: during a set term

Part II has no section that lets a landlord raise the rent during a set term. The rent is what the lease says. Quote the rent clause and any clause on changing the lease.

1. **No clause allows it** (see "What the lease adds").
2. **The tenant did not agree.**
   - They signed a change: the rent is what they signed, if it meets the lease's clause on changes.
   - They said yes without signing: not settled whether that changes the rent. One: a rental agreement can include an "oral agreement for a duration of less than 1 year" (83.43(13)). The other: a lease clause requiring a signed change still governs.
   - They paid it without signing: this option's plain answer does not apply. Start from "If the tenant already paid it", which is not settled.

Both met: the landlord cannot change the rent alone before the lease ends. Say so plainly. The tenant keeps paying the lease's rent, in full and on time, and can tell the landlord in writing that they do not agree, quoting the rent clause and sending it the way the lease's notice clause says. It helps to keep the letter, the lease, and proof of each payment. Say the risk too: see "If the landlord treats it as unpaid rent". The landlord can ask for more when the term ends (option 2).

## Option 2: a higher rent for a new term

Part II names no right to renew at the same rent and no limit on what a landlord may ask for a new term. Say so plainly. The lease's rent stands through lease_end_date whatever the offer says. From there:

- **Agree:** the new rent starts with the new term. Say what they should read before signing: the rent, the term, and any new charge.
- **Leave at the end:** load lease_ending for any notice the lease asks for.
- **Stay without agreeing:** load lease_ending. Staying without permission can mean "double the amount of rent due" (83.58). Read the lease's clause on staying after the end; if it makes the tenancy month to month, say what it says, and option 3 applies from then.

## Option 3: no set end date

Part II sets no notice for this and does not say a landlord may change the rent alone, so what an increase takes is not settled. Give all three readings and choose none. Quote any lease clause on signed changes.

- One: a landlord that can end the tenancy only on 83.57's notice can change the rent only with the same notice, written and delivered a way 83.56(4) names, for month to month "not less than 30 days’ notice prior to the end of any monthly period" (83.57(3)).
- Two: no section sets a notice, so none in particular is needed, and the tenant can pay it or leave.
- Three: 83.57 only lets a party end the tenancy, so the rent changes only if the tenant agrees, and a landlord that wants more must end the tenancy on that notice and offer new terms. A lease clause requiring a signed change points this way.

The date: count_days(period_end, -N), with N from 83.57: 30 for month to month (83.57(3)), and for other rent periods the number in 83.57(1), (2), or (4). Set increase_delivered beside it. The ways 83.56(4) names are mailing, a true copy by hand, e-mail under the signed addendum in 83.505(1), or, if the tenant is away, a copy left at the home.

- In writing, a way named, and on or before that date: in time under readings one and two. Say so plainly. Under reading three the letter alone still does not change the rent.
- Later than that, or spoken, or by text or portal: not good for that date under reading one, enough under reading two, and no change under reading three. Whether a late notice works for the next period under reading one is not settled, as lease_ending says of a late notice to end a tenancy; its date is count_days(next_period_end, -N).

Under every reading the landlord may end the tenancy on that notice: it "may be terminated by either party giving written notice in the manner provided in s. 83.56 (4)" (83.57), and no reason is named. Say so, so the tenant knows what refusing can lead to.

The tenant's choices. Name no choice as the safest; say what each risks.

- Pay the new rent. See "If the tenant already paid it" for what paying may mean.
- Pay the old rent and say in writing why. See "If the landlord treats it as unpaid rent".
- End the tenancy: load lease_ending. The last day to give notice is count_days(period_end, -N), or count_days(next_period_end, -N) if that has passed.

## Option 4: retaliation

"It is unlawful for a landlord to discriminatorily increase a tenant’s rent or decrease services to a tenant, or to bring or threaten to bring an action for possession or other civil action, primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant." (83.64(1)).

All of these must be met.

1. **Something the tenant did first.** "Examples of conduct for which the landlord may not retaliate include, but are not limited to, situations where:" (83.64(1)) they complained to a code agency (83.64(1)(a)), took part in a tenant organization (83.64(1)(b)), complained to the landlord under 83.56(1) (83.64(1)(c)), ended a lease as a servicemember (83.64(1)(d)), paid rent to an association after its demand (83.64(1)(e)), or used fair housing rights (83.64(1)(f)). Fair housing law itself is outside this tool. Another step, like an ordinary repair request: not settled. One: the list is only examples, so it can count. The other: it counts only if it is like the named ones, and a request that says nothing about ending the lease is not 83.56(1)'s complaint.
2. **Good faith.** "In order for the tenant to raise the defense of retaliatory conduct, the tenant must have acted in good faith." (83.64(1)). "“Good faith” means honesty in fact in the conduct or transaction concerned." (83.43(8)). Applying that is for a court.
3. **Treated differently.** "“Discrimination” under this section means that a tenant is being treated differently as to the rent charged, the services rendered, or the action being taken by the landlord, which shall be a prerequisite to a finding of retaliatory conduct." (83.64(4)). Set what they know of other tenants' rent beside the words. The same increase for everyone points against it; say so plainly. If they do not know, say that is the fact to find out.
4. **Primarily to retaliate.** This is the landlord's motive, for a court. An increase that followed such a step is not retaliation for that reason alone. Give the dates as the tenant gave them; never count the days between them.

What it gives: "Evidence of retaliatory conduct may be raised by the tenant as a defense in any action brought against him or her for possession." (83.64(2)), unless "the landlord proves that the eviction is for good cause." (83.64(3)), whose examples include "good faith actions for nonpayment of rent" (83.64(3)). So not paying the new rent can weaken it; say so.

What the tenant can do about an increase alone, before any case: not settled. One: 83.64(2) makes it only a defense, so there is nothing to raise until a case. The other: 83.64(1) makes the increase unlawful, "Any right or duty declared in this part is enforceable by civil action." (83.54), and a party may recover damages for a failure to comply with "this part" (83.55).

## If the tenant already paid it

"if the tenant pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord" (83.56(5)(a)), the tenant "waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." (83.56(5)(a)).

Ask what they knew when they paid, and set it beside "actual knowledge" (83.56(5)(a)). Whether paying a raised rent gives up the extra, or changes the rent from then on, is not settled, so going back to the lease's rent and getting the extra back are not settled either. Start the answer there. One: paying with knowledge gives up a suit over those months and may show the tenant agreed. The other: an increase the lease never allowed is not rent "due" (83.43(12)), a clause requiring a signed change still stands, and the extra can be claimed under 83.55, with each later month a "subsequent or continuing noncompliance" (83.56(5)(a)). Amounts and court steps are outside this tool; do not total them.

## If the landlord treats it as unpaid rent

- **A written demand.** "If the tenant fails to pay rent when due and the default continues for 3 days, excluding Saturday, Sunday, and legal holidays, after delivery of written demand by the landlord for payment of the rent or possession of the premises, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement." (83.56(3)). This tool does not count those days; the demand states them. Say not to ignore it.
- **Taking the old rent.** A landlord "does not waive the right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance by accepting partial rent for the period." (83.56(5)(a)). So taking it does not mean the landlord gave in. "If partial rent is accepted after posting the notice for nonpayment, the landlord must:" (83.56(5)(a)) give a receipt with the date, the amount, and the balance before filing; or put the amount in the court's registry on filing; or post a new 3-day notice (83.56(5)(a)). Whether the lease's rent is "partial" at all is the dispute.
- **No court case, no removal.** "The landlord shall not recover possession of a dwelling unit except:" (83.59(3)) through a court case, or when the tenant gave up or abandoned the home (83.59(3)). The landlord "shall not prevent the tenant from gaining reasonable access to the dwelling unit by any means" (83.67(2)).
- **A case filed.** Say this first. The tenant must pay into the registry "the accrued rent as alleged in the complaint or as determined by the court and the rent that accrues during the pendency of the proceeding, when due." (83.60(2)). "Failure of the tenant to pay the rent into the registry of the court or to file a motion to determine the amount of rent to be paid into the registry within 5 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays, after the date of service of process constitutes an absolute waiver of the tenant’s defenses other than payment, and the landlord is entitled to an immediate default judgment for removal of the tenant with a writ of possession to issue without further notice or hearing thereon." (83.60(2)). When the amount is what they dispute, the motion is the way to say so: "If a motion to determine rent is filed, documentation in support of the allegation that the rent as alleged in the complaint is in error is required." (83.60(2)). A tenant with subsidized rent deposits "only that portion of the full rent for which they are responsible" (83.60(2)). Give the 5 days and what they leave out, but never a calendar date for them; "The clerk shall notify the tenant of such requirement in the summons." (83.60(2)).
- **Defenses.** The tenant "may raise any other defense, whether legal or equitable, that he or she may have, including the defense of retaliatory conduct in accordance with s. 83.64" (83.60(1)(a)). The winner may recover attorney fees and court costs (83.48). Other court steps are outside this tool.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Stating a notice period or a cap for rent increases as the law.
- Saying a landlord may raise the rent during a set term with no clause and no agreement, or calling the lease's own rent steps an increase.
- Treating 83.57's 30 days as settled for an increase, saying flatly that no notice is needed, or saying flatly that a letter alone changes the rent with no set end date.
- Saying an increase is retaliation because it followed a complaint, or leaving out good faith or being treated differently.
- Telling a tenant they can stop paying rent altogether, explaining a case without 83.60(2), or giving a calendar date for its 5 days.
- Applying a local rent rule from memory.
- Writing any date count_days did not give you, or counting how long something has lasted or how long until a date. Setting a date from the facts beside a date count_days gave is not counting.

answer:
**Short answer:** Whether you can go back to $1,050 and get the extra money back is not settled. Your lease sets the rent at $1,050 through July 31, 2026. It also says changes must be in a signed writing, and you signed nothing. The landlord could not raise the rent alone during the lease. But you paid $1,150 for March and April knowing it was higher, and that may cost you the right to claim those two payments back. Courts could read it either way. If you go back to $1,050, the landlord may treat the $100 gap as unpaid rent. Has the landlord sent you anything in writing about rent since March, such as a demand or a late notice?

DETAILS

### Could the landlord raise your rent in the middle of the lease?
Your lease runs from August 1, 2025 to July 31, 2026 (lease ¶3), and the new rent was to start March 1, 2026. That falls inside the lease term.
- Lease ¶4 sets the rent: "Rent is $1,050.00 per month."
- Lease ¶10 says the lease "may be changed only in writing signed by Landlord and Tenant."
- Nothing in the lease lets the landlord raise the rent during the term.
- Part II of the statute has no section that lets a landlord raise rent during a set term. It also has no rule on how much notice an increase needs, and no cap on increases.

You signed nothing and only started paying the higher amount. So the lease's rent was still $1,050 for March and April.

### Did paying $1,150 change that?
This is the part that is not settled. You told me you knew the amount was higher when you paid, but you hadn't read the lease. There are two readings.
- **Reading one: paying gave up the claim.** Under 83.56(5)(a), "if the tenant pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord," the tenant "waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." On this reading, you knew the amount had gone up, so you may not be able to recover March and April. Your payments may also be taken as agreeing to the new rent. Section 83.43(13) says a rental agreement can include an "oral agreement for a duration of less than 1 year."
- **Reading two: the extra was never owed.** Rent is what is "due" under the rental agreement (83.43(12)). The lease never allowed an increase, and ¶10 still requires a signed change. On this reading, the extra can be claimed under 83.55. Each later month at $1,150 would be a new "subsequent or continuing noncompliance" (83.56(5)(a)), which the waiver language does not cover.

Whether "actual knowledge" fits what you knew is for a court to decide. I can't say which reading a court would pick. I also can't give amounts or court steps.

### Can you go back to $1,050 starting now?
Nothing in the statute stops you from paying what your lease says. The risk is that the landlord treats $1,050 as short rent.
- A written demand can start a short deadline. Under 83.56(3), if rent isn't paid and "the default continues for 3 days, excluding Saturday, Sunday, and legal holidays, after delivery of written demand," the landlord "may terminate the rental agreement." If you get a demand, don't ignore it.
- Under 83.56(5)(a), a landlord "does not waive the right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance by accepting partial rent for the period." Whether $1,050 counts as "partial" is the dispute.
- The landlord can't remove you without a court case (83.59(3)) and can't lock you out (83.67(2)).
- If a case were filed, you would have to pay rent into the court's registry or file a motion to set the amount within 5 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays and legal holidays, after being served (83.60(2)). Missing that deadline waives your defenses other than payment.

### How could you put your position in writing?
You can tell the landlord in writing that you don't agree to the increase. Quote lease ¶4 and ¶10. Lease ¶7 says written notices to the landlord go "by hand to the office at 1840 SW 13th Street, Suite A" or by certified mail to that address. Keep a copy of the letter, your lease, and proof of each payment.

### What happens after July 31, 2026?
The landlord can ask for a higher rent for a new term. Part II names no right to renew at the same rent. The $1,050 rent stands through July 31, 2026 (lease ¶3). Lease ¶9 makes the tenancy month to month only if you stay after July 31 "with Landlord's written consent."

Loaded rent_increased. Its instructions:

# Rent increased

Rests on 83.46 (rent, tenancies with no set term), 83.43 (what rent is, good faith), 83.57 (ending a tenancy with no set term), 83.64 (retaliation), 83.425 (local rules), 83.56 (unpaid rent, rent paid, notices), 83.60 (if sued), 83.55 and 83.54 (damages, suits), 83.44 and 83.45 (good faith, unfair clauses), 83.48 (attorney fees), 83.51 and 83.491 (trash, a fee in place of a deposit), 83.59 and 83.67 (no lockout), and 83.505 (e-mail notices). Read a section in full with get_statute_section.

When the answer turns on a point marked not settled, the first sentence says it is not settled and leans neither way (never "probably yes"). Every point marked not settled gets all its readings, and you choose none.

## First, whether this applies

- Load who_the_law_covers, unless the facts already hold school_housing.
- Part II has no section that sets how much notice a rent increase needs, and none that limits how much rent may go up. Say so plainly when asked. Never state a notice period or a cap as the law.
- Local rules: "The regulation of residential tenancies, the landlord-tenant relationship, and all other matters covered under this part are preempted to the state." (83.425), and the section supersedes local rules on matters including "fees charged by the landlord; or notice requirements." (83.425). The stored text holds no local rent rule. Never apply one from memory.
- Rent paid through a program (a voucher, public housing): the program's own rules are not stored. Say they may limit this, and that they are outside this tool.
- The increase comes with an offer to renew, or the tenant would rather leave: load lease_ending too.

## What the lease adds

Read the whole lease, addenda included, for: the rent, the term, any clause on the rent changing, how the lease may be changed, any charges, staying after the end, and how notices go to the landlord. Quote each clause and cite it.

- **Rent steps set in the lease from the start** (so much until a date, then more): that is the lease's rent, not an increase. Say so.
- **A clause letting the landlord raise the rent during the term:** set the increase beside the clause's conditions (how much notice, how it is given, how much, how often). If it gives a number of days N: the last day to give notice for the start date named is count_days(new_rent_starts, -N), and the earliest start from the notice given is count_days(increase_delivered, N). All conditions met: the rent goes up as the lease says; say so plainly. Any not met: the clause does not support this increase on these terms; say so plainly. The rent stays where it is for now and the tenant keeps paying it, but the landlord can still raise it by meeting the clause, so say that too. Option 1's plain answer is for a lease with no such clause. A clause with no limit at all: say what it says, that it carries "an obligation of good faith in its performance or enforcement." (83.44), and that whether it is unfair enough to be "unconscionable" (83.45(1)) is for a court.
- **A new charge** (an amenity fee, a trash fee): the same questions as for rent. The lease provides it: owed as the lease says. It does not: during a set term the landlord cannot add it alone, any more than it can raise the rent. A fee counts as rent only if it is "designated as rent in a written rental agreement." (83.43(12)). That matters because a demand under 83.56(3) and the registry under 83.60(2) speak of rent.
  - Trash: in a unit other than a single-family home or duplex, "Garbage removal and outside receptacles therefor." (83.51(2)(a)) falls to the landlord "Unless otherwise agreed in writing" (83.51(2)(a)), though the rental agreement may put the charges on the tenant (83.51(2)(e)).
  - A fee in place of a security deposit: "The amount of the fee, which may not be increased during the term of the rental agreement." (83.491(4)(a)).

## Facts the answer turns on

Read the lease first. Ask the tenant only plain facts, one or two at a time. Note each fact with note_fact under these names, dates written YYYY-MM-DD; a date counts only once the tenant has confirmed it.

- new_rent: the new amount. increase_delivered: the date word of it reached them, and how it came (handed over, mail, portal, text, spoken). new_rent_starts: the date it is said to start.
- lease_end_date: the date the lease ends, if it has one. period_end: the last day of the rent period before the new rent starts. next_period_end: the last day of the rent period after that.
- agreed: whether they signed anything or said yes. paid_new_rent: whether they have paid the new amount, for which months, and what they knew about the lease when they paid.
- complaint_date: the date of any complaint or similar step before the increase, and what it was. others_rent: what they know about other tenants' rent.
- rent_demand: any written demand for rent, and its date. eviction_filed: whether a case has been filed, and whether they were served.

## Which kind of increase

Settle this first. With a set end date, call count_days(lease_end_date, 0) and set new_rent_starts beside the date it gives.

- A set end date, and the new rent starts on or before it: option 1.
- A set end date, and the new rent starts after it: option 2.
- No set end date, or the tenant stayed on after a set term with the landlord's permission: option 3. With no term stated, "the duration is determined by the periods for which the rent is payable." (83.46(2)). Stayed on without permission, or in doubt: load lease_ending too.

Any kind: option 4 if the tenant did something first that the landlord may be answering, such as a complaint or joining a tenant group, and the two parts after it if they fit.

## Option 1: during a set term

Part II has no section that lets a landlord raise the rent during a set term. The rent is what the lease says. Quote the rent clause and any clause on changing the lease.

1. **No clause allows it** (see "What the lease adds").
2. **The tenant did not agree.**
   - They signed a change: the rent is what they signed, if it meets the lease's clause on changes.
   - They said yes without signing: not settled whether that changes the rent. One: a rental agreement can include an "oral agreement for a duration of less than 1 year" (83.43(13)). The other: a lease clause requiring a signed change still governs.
   - They paid it without signing: this option's plain answer does not apply. Start from "If the tenant already paid it", which is not settled.

Both met: the landlord cannot change the rent alone before the lease ends. Say so plainly. The tenant keeps paying the lease's rent, in full and on time, and can tell the landlord in writing that they do not agree, quoting the rent clause and sending it the way the lease's notice clause says. It helps to keep the letter, the lease, and proof of each payment. Say the risk too: see "If the landlord treats it as unpaid rent". The landlord can ask for more when the term ends (option 2).

## Option 2: a higher rent for a new term

Part II names no right to renew at the same rent and no limit on what a landlord may ask for a new term. Say so plainly. The lease's rent stands through lease_end_date whatever the offer says. From there:

- **Agree:** the new rent starts with the new term. Say what they should read before signing: the rent, the term, and any new charge.
- **Leave at the end:** load lease_ending for any notice the lease asks for.
- **Stay without agreeing:** load lease_ending. Staying without permission can mean "double the amount of rent due" (83.58). Read the lease's clause on staying after the end; if it makes the tenancy month to month, say what it says, and option 3 applies from then.

## Option 3: no set end date

Part II sets no notice for this and does not say a landlord may change the rent alone, so what an increase takes is not settled. Give all three readings and choose none. Quote any lease clause on signed changes.

- One: a landlord that can end the tenancy only on 83.57's notice can change the rent only with the same notice, written and delivered a way 83.56(4) names, for month to month "not less than 30 days’ notice prior to the end of any monthly period" (83.57(3)).
- Two: no section sets a notice, so none in particular is needed, and the tenant can pay it or leave.
- Three: 83.57 only lets a party end the tenancy, so the rent changes only if the tenant agrees, and a landlord that wants more must end the tenancy on that notice and offer new terms. A lease clause requiring a signed change points this way.

The date: count_days(period_end, -N), with N from 83.57: 30 for month to month (83.57(3)), and for other rent periods the number in 83.57(1), (2), or (4). Set increase_delivered beside it. The ways 83.56(4) names are mailing, a true copy by hand, e-mail under the signed addendum in 83.505(1), or, if the tenant is away, a copy left at the home.

- In writing, a way named, and on or before that date: in time under readings one and two. Say so plainly. Under reading three the letter alone still does not change the rent.
- Later than that, or spoken, or by text or portal: not good for that date under reading one, enough under reading two, and no change under reading three. Whether a late notice works for the next period under reading one is not settled, as lease_ending says of a late notice to end a tenancy; its date is count_days(next_period_end, -N).

Under every reading the landlord may end the tenancy on that notice: it "may be terminated by either party giving written notice in the manner provided in s. 83.56 (4)" (83.57), and no reason is named. Say so, so the tenant knows what refusing can lead to.

The tenant's choices. Name no choice as the safest; say what each risks.

- Pay the new rent. See "If the tenant already paid it" for what paying may mean.
- Pay the old rent and say in writing why. See "If the landlord treats it as unpaid rent".
- End the tenancy: load lease_ending. The last day to give notice is count_days(period_end, -N), or count_days(next_period_end, -N) if that has passed.

## Option 4: retaliation

"It is unlawful for a landlord to discriminatorily increase a tenant’s rent or decrease services to a tenant, or to bring or threaten to bring an action for possession or other civil action, primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant." (83.64(1)).

All of these must be met.

1. **Something the tenant did first.** "Examples of conduct for which the landlord may not retaliate include, but are not limited to, situations where:" (83.64(1)) they complained to a code agency (83.64(1)(a)), took part in a tenant organization (83.64(1)(b)), complained to the landlord under 83.56(1) (83.64(1)(c)), ended a lease as a servicemember (83.64(1)(d)), paid rent to an association after its demand (83.64(1)(e)), or used fair housing rights (83.64(1)(f)). Fair housing law itself is outside this tool. Another step, like an ordinary repair request: not settled. One: the list is only examples, so it can count. The other: it counts only if it is like the named ones, and a request that says nothing about ending the lease is not 83.56(1)'s complaint.
2. **Good faith.** "In order for the tenant to raise the defense of retaliatory conduct, the tenant must have acted in good faith." (83.64(1)). "“Good faith” means honesty in fact in the conduct or transaction concerned." (83.43(8)). Applying that is for a court.
3. **Treated differently.** "“Discrimination” under this section means that a tenant is being treated differently as to the rent charged, the services rendered, or the action being taken by the landlord, which shall be a prerequisite to a finding of retaliatory conduct." (83.64(4)). Set what they know of other tenants' rent beside the words. The same increase for everyone points against it; say so plainly. If they do not know, say that is the fact to find out.
4. **Primarily to retaliate.** This is the landlord's motive, for a court. An increase that followed such a step is not retaliation for that reason alone. Give the dates as the tenant gave them; never count the days between them.

What it gives: "Evidence of retaliatory conduct may be raised by the tenant as a defense in any action brought against him or her for possession." (83.64(2)), unless "the landlord proves that the eviction is for good cause." (83.64(3)), whose examples include "good faith actions for nonpayment of rent" (83.64(3)). So not paying the new rent can weaken it; say so.

What the tenant can do about an increase alone, before any case: not settled. One: 83.64(2) makes it only a defense, so there is nothing to raise until a case. The other: 83.64(1) makes the increase unlawful, "Any right or duty declared in this part is enforceable by civil action." (83.54), and a party may recover damages for a failure to comply with "this part" (83.55).

## If the tenant already paid it

"if the tenant pays rent with actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord" (83.56(5)(a)), the tenant "waives his or her right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance, but not for any subsequent or continuing noncompliance." (83.56(5)(a)).

Ask what they knew when they paid, and set it beside "actual knowledge" (83.56(5)(a)). Whether paying a raised rent gives up the extra, or changes the rent from then on, is not settled, so going back to the lease's rent and getting the extra back are not settled either. Start the answer there. One: paying with knowledge gives up a suit over those months and may show the tenant agreed. The other: an increase the lease never allowed is not rent "due" (83.43(12)), a clause requiring a signed change still stands, and the extra can be claimed under 83.55, with each later month a "subsequent or continuing noncompliance" (83.56(5)(a)). Amounts and court steps are outside this tool; do not total them.

## If the landlord treats it as unpaid rent

- **A written demand.** "If the tenant fails to pay rent when due and the default continues for 3 days, excluding Saturday, Sunday, and legal holidays, after delivery of written demand by the landlord for payment of the rent or possession of the premises, the landlord may terminate the rental agreement." (83.56(3)). This tool does not count those days; the demand states them. Say not to ignore it.
- **Taking the old rent.** A landlord "does not waive the right to terminate the rental agreement or to bring a civil action for that noncompliance by accepting partial rent for the period." (83.56(5)(a)). So taking it does not mean the landlord gave in. "If partial rent is accepted after posting the notice for nonpayment, the landlord must:" (83.56(5)(a)) give a receipt with the date, the amount, and the balance before filing; or put the amount in the court's registry on filing; or post a new 3-day notice (83.56(5)(a)). Whether the lease's rent is "partial" at all is the dispute.
- **No court case, no removal.** "The landlord shall not recover possession of a dwelling unit except:" (83.59(3)) through a court case, or when the tenant gave up or abandoned the home (83.59(3)). The landlord "shall not prevent the tenant from gaining reasonable access to the dwelling unit by any means" (83.67(2)).
- **A case filed.** Say this first. The tenant must pay into the registry "the accrued rent as alleged in the complaint or as determined by the court and the rent that accrues during the pendency of the proceeding, when due." (83.60(2)). "Failure of the tenant to pay the rent into the registry of the court or to file a motion to determine the amount of rent to be paid into the registry within 5 days, excluding Saturdays, Sundays, and legal holidays, after the date of service of process constitutes an absolute waiver of the tenant’s defenses other than payment, and the landlord is entitled to an immediate default judgment for removal of the tenant with a writ of possession to issue without further notice or hearing thereon." (83.60(2)). When the amount is what they dispute, the motion is the way to say so: "If a motion to determine rent is filed, documentation in support of the allegation that the rent as alleged in the complaint is in error is required." (83.60(2)). A tenant with subsidized rent deposits "only that portion of the full rent for which they are responsible" (83.60(2)). Give the 5 days and what they leave out, but never a calendar date for them; "The clerk shall notify the tenant of such requirement in the summons." (83.60(2)).
- **Defenses.** The tenant "may raise any other defense, whether legal or equitable, that he or she may have, including the defense of retaliatory conduct in accordance with s. 83.64" (83.60(1)(a)). The winner may recover attorney fees and court costs (83.48). Other court steps are outside this tool.

## Mistakes to avoid

- Stating a notice period or a cap for rent increases as the law.
- Saying a landlord may raise the rent during a set term with no clause and no agreement, or calling the lease's own rent steps an increase.
- Treating 83.57's 30 days as settled for an increase, saying flatly that no notice is needed, or saying flatly that a letter alone changes the rent with no set end date.
- Saying an increase is retaliation because it followed a complaint, or leaving out good faith or being treated differently.
- Telling a tenant they can stop paying rent altogether, explaining a case without 83.60(2), or giving a calendar date for its 5 days.
- Applying a local rent rule from memory.
- Writing any date count_days did not give you, or counting how long something has lasted or how long until a date. Setting a date from the facts beside a date count_days gave is not counting.

answer:
**Short answer:** It's not settled whether the increase is valid, and the answer depends on which of three readings of the law a court takes. Florida's landlord-tenant law (part II) doesn't say how much notice a rent increase needs, and it doesn't cap how much rent can go up. If a court applies the 30-day notice for ending a month-to-month tenancy, your March 20 letter was too late for April 1. Under another reading, no set notice is needed. Under a third, your rent can't change unless you agree, and you haven't agreed. In the meantime, you haven't agreed to or paid the new rent, and nothing in your lease allows the landlord to raise it alone. Your landlord can also end a month-to-month tenancy with proper written notice, so refusing the increase carries that risk. Do you want to stay in the apartment, or are you thinking of moving out?

DETAILS

### Does the law set a notice period or a cap for a rent increase?
No. Part II has no section on how much notice an increase needs, and none that limits the amount. Local rules can't fill the gap either. The law says these matters are "preempted to the state" (83.425). I haven't applied any local rent rule.

### What does your lease say?
- Your tenancy is "month to month until ended by Tenant or Landlord" (lease §3).
- Rent is "$1,050.00 per month" (lease §4).
- The lease has no clause that lets the landlord change the rent during the tenancy.
- The lease "may be changed only in writing signed by Landlord and Tenant" (lease §10).
- You told me you did not agree to the increase, and you haven't paid the new amount.

### Was the letter on time? Three readings
Part II doesn't say what an increase takes, so I can't pick one reading.

1. **The 30-day reading.** A landlord who can end a month-to-month tenancy only with 83.57(3)'s notice can change the rent only with the same notice. That notice must be "not less than 30 days' notice prior to the end of any monthly period," and it must be written and delivered in a way 83.56(4) names.
   - Handing you a true copy counts as a way 83.56(4) names. Your lease (§8) says notices go "to the apartment while Tenant lives there."
   - The last day to give notice for an April 1 start was March 1, and that date has passed. Your letter came March 20, so it was late for April under this reading.
   - Whether a late notice still works for the next rent period is not settled. That period ends April 30, and its 30-day cutoff is March 31.
2. **The no-set-notice reading.** No section sets a notice for increases, so none in particular is needed. You could pay the new rent or leave.
3. **The agreement reading.** Section 83.57 only lets a party end the tenancy. Under this view, the rent changes only if you agree. A landlord who wants more would have to end the tenancy on proper notice and offer new terms. Your lease's signed-changes clause (§10) points this way.

### What can the landlord do if you refuse?
Under every reading, either side can end a month-to-month tenancy. The law says it "may be terminated by either party giving written notice in the manner provided in s. 83.56 (4)" (83.57), and it names no required reason. The landlord could send a proper 30-day notice instead of relying on the rent letter.

### What are your choices?
I'm not naming any of these as the safest.

- **Pay $1,200.** Paying with "actual knowledge of a noncompliance by the landlord" can give up your right to sue over that noncompliance (83.56(5)(a)). It could also be used to show you accepted the new rent. Whether you could later get the extra back is not settled.
- **Pay $1,050 and explain in writing.** You can say you don't agree and point to lease §4 and §10. Under your lease (§7), deliver it by hand to Suite A at 1840 SW 13th Street or send it there by certified mail. Keep a copy and proof of each payment.
  - The risk is that the landlord may treat the $1,050 as unpaid rent. A written demand for rent gives you 3 days, not counting weekends and court holidays, before the landlord may end the tenancy (83.56(3)). Don't ignore that demand.
  - The landlord can't remove you without a court case (83.59(3)) and can't lock you out (83.67(2)).
  - If the landlord sues, you must pay the rent into the court registry or file a motion about the amount within 5 days after being served, not counting weekends and court holidays. If you don't, you lose your defenses other than payment (83.60(2)).
- **Move out.** To end a month-to-month tenancy you give your own written notice of at least 30 days before the end of a monthly period (83.57(3)). For the period ending April 30, the last day is March 31. Under your lease (§7), deliver it by hand to the office or by certified mail.

### Could this be retaliation?
Retaliation is unlawful, and it includes raising rent "primarily because the landlord is retaliating against the tenant" (83.64(1)). It usually requires that you first did something protected, such as complaining to a code agency or to the landlord about a repair, and that you acted in good faith. It also requires that you were treated differently from other tenants (83.64(4)). Nothing you've told me suggests any of that. If you made a complaint before the letter, or you know other tenants didn't get an increase, tell me. Those facts would change this part of the answer.
